hook.support: Think of someone great to listen to. Now think of someone boring. They might say the same words. The difference is **how** they say them.
hook.core: Think of someone who's great to listen to — a coach, a YouTuber, a teacher. Now think of someone who sends you to sleep. They might be saying the same words. The difference is **how** they say it: where they look, how they stand, how fast they talk.

why.support: In a job interview or a meeting, people judge you fast. Before your words, they notice your eyes, hands and voice. You can control those.
why.core: In a job interview, a team meeting or a debate, people decide whether to trust you in seconds — often before they've judged your words. You can't control everything, but you **can** control your eyes, your hands, your pace and your voice.
why.extend: Listeners judge confidence fast, often from delivery rather than content. Body language, eye contact, gesture, pace and tone can back up your message or undercut it. You can practise, film and improve them.

articles.title: Five tools you always carry

body.support:
When you speak, people get three things: your **words**, your **body** and your **voice**. If they don't match, people believe your body and voice.

You have five tools:

1. **Stance.** Stand still on both feet. Don't sway.
2. **Eye contact.** Look at people. Not the floor.
3. **Gestures.** Use your hands to show what you mean. Then let them rest.
4. **Pace.** Slow down for big points. **Pause** before them.
5. **Tone.** Let your voice go up and down. A flat voice sounds bored.

You can get better at this. **Film yourself.** Watch it. Change one thing. Try again.
body.core:
When you give your opinion out loud, your audience gets three things at once: your **words**, your **body** and your **voice**. If they don't match, people believe the body and voice.

You carry five delivery tools everywhere:

1. **Stance.** Stand steady with your weight on both feet. Swaying and shuffling look nervous.
2. **Eye contact.** Look at people, not the floor or your notes. Move your eyes around the group.
3. **Gestures.** Use your hands to show meaning: count off three points, show something big. Then rest them, not in your pockets.
4. **Pace and pauses.** Nerves make you rush. Slow down for your most important point, and **pause** before it.
5. **Tone.** Let your voice rise and fall. A flat voice sounds bored, even when you're not.

Delivery is a **skill**, not a personality. The fastest way to improve is to **film yourself**, watch it back, change **one** thing, and try again. Everyone hates watching themselves at first. Do it anyway.
body.extend:
When you present an opinion aloud, your audience receives three channels at once: **verbal** (your words), **visual** (your body) and **vocal** (your voice). When they conflict — confident words, nervous body — audiences tend to trust the body and voice.

Five delivery tools are always available:

1. **Stance**: grounded, balanced posture signals confidence; swaying or shifting signals nerves.
2. **Eye contact**: sustained, shared around the room, it builds connection and credibility.
3. **Gesture**: purposeful hand movements (counting points, showing scale) reinforce meaning. Fidgeting distracts from it.
4. **Pace and pause**: nerves speed you up. Deliberately slowing for key points, and pausing before them, signals importance.
5. **Intonation**: variation in pitch and emphasis carries emotion and meaning. A monotone undercuts even a strong argument.

Delivery is a trainable skill, not a fixed trait. The most effective practice is deliberate: film, review against criteria, change one thing, repeat.

caseStudies.title: The debate people watched — and the one they heard

body.support:
In **1960**, two men running for US president had a debate. It was the first one on **TV**. Some people listened on the **radio** instead.

Nixon had been sick. He looked pale and sweaty. Kennedy looked calm and looked at the camera.

A famous story says: people on **TV** thought Kennedy won, but people on **radio** thought Nixon won.

In 2003, a researcher tested it. People who **watched** were more likely to say Kennedy won. But people who only **listened** also picked Kennedy more.

So how you look matters. But famous stories need checking too.
body.core:
On **26 September 1960**, US presidential candidates **John F. Kennedy** and **Richard Nixon** held the first presidential debate shown on **TV**. Many people also listened on **radio**.

Nixon had been sick. He looked pale and sweaty and glanced away from the camera. Kennedy looked calm, tanned and spoke straight to viewers.

A famous story grew: **TV viewers** thought Kennedy won, but **radio listeners** thought Nixon won. It's repeated everywhere. But it rests mostly on **one small poll**.

In 2003, a researcher, **James Druckman**, tested it. He showed some people the debate on video and played others only the sound. The video group was **more likely** to say Kennedy won. But **both groups** picked Kennedy more often.

So: how you look and sound does seem to matter. But even famous stories need checking.
body.extend:
On **26 September 1960**, **John F. Kennedy** and **Richard Nixon** took part in the first US presidential debate shown on **TV**. Millions watched; others listened on **radio**.

Nixon had been sick. He looked pale and sweaty, and often looked away from the camera. Kennedy looked calm and spoke straight to viewers.

A famous claim followed: **TV viewers** thought Kennedy won, while **radio listeners** backed Nixon. It's repeated in textbooks and training courses. Yet it rests mostly on one poll with only a small group of radio listeners.

In 2003, the researcher **James Druckman** tested the idea. He showed some people the video and played others only the sound. Viewers were clearly **more likely** to rate Kennedy the winner, so image seemed to matter. But **both** groups preferred Kennedy, which doesn't fit the strong version of the story.

Two lessons follow. Delivery shapes how people judge a speaker. And good stories about persuasion need checking like any other evidence.

teacher.overview: Students learn five delivery tools (stance, eye contact, gesture, pace and pauses, tone) and use them deliberately when giving an opinion. They mark up a cue card, film themselves before and after practice, and rate the change. The case study is the 1960 Kennedy–Nixon TV debate, including the 2003 experiment that tested the famous story.
prep: Check your school's rules on students filming each other; students can film themselves only, or use school devices.
Find a quiet space for filming (corridors, breakout rooms).
Optional: a 60-second clip of a confident speaker and a nervous one to compare.

teacher.answers:
**Sort:** reading off phone — hurts; pausing — helps; hands in pockets — hurts; counting reasons — helps; swaying — hurts; looking around the room — helps.

**Cue card:** 1 look up (eye contact); 2 slow down (pace); 3 count on fingers (gesture); 4 pause; 5 eye contact across the room; 6 stance/breathing reminder.

**Case study:** Nixon pale, sweaty, glancing away; Kennedy calm, looked at camera. Story: TV viewers picked Kennedy, radio listeners Nixon. 2003 test: video viewers more likely to pick Kennedy, but both groups favoured Kennedy, so the strong story is exaggerated.

Druckman (2003), The Power of Television Images — Journal of Politics (PDF)

realityCheck: **Filming yourself is the hardest ask in this course.** Many students will refuse at first. Offer options: film alone, audio only, or perform for you privately. Never show videos to the class without permission.
**Anxiety is real.** For some students, speaking up is genuinely distressing. Keep the stakes low (60 seconds, one improvement) and praise the improvement, not the polish.
**Cultural differences matter.** Eye contact norms vary across cultures, including for some First Nations students. Frame the tools as choices for this audience, not rules about right and wrong.
**The case study is American and from 1960.** It lands better with a 1-minute clip, and the twist that the famous story is exaggerated usually gets a reaction.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's VPC at its best: practical, visible improvement in one lesson. Allow time; filming always takes longer than planned.
